entries.claim: A prototype pollution report is validated only when a probe sent in one request changes an object built by a different, later request; a change reproduced only within the payload's own request does not demonstrate prototype pollution.
steps: Prove the sink reads a file at all BEFORE testing traversal: fetch a file you KNOW exists on the target and confirm real content comes back.
If you cannot get a known-good read, there is no traversal finding to report — the sink is not proven.
Then apply the traversal value and confirm the returned content is from OUTSIDE the intended directory. Content, not status code.
Reject any result where only the status line differs: proxies, error handlers and WAFs produce status differentials with no file ever read.
variation: - **Do two layers disagree about the same bytes?** — single: **do** one parser sees the request; **observe** a consistent rejection or acceptance.
- **What sits between client and sink?** — http2: **do** negotiate h2/h2c; **observe** frame-level parsing differences.
- **AS whom are you testing?** — low_priv: **do** send as your lowest-privilege account; **observe** whether the response differs from anonymous.
- **What PROVES it, beyond a status code?** — differential: **do** compare against a control that differs in one variable; **observe** the difference the control did not produce.
escalation: No effect raw? Walk the encoding ladder: raw -> percent-encoded -> double-encoded -> look-alike separators, one rung at a time, never all at once.
Still flat? You have proven the sink is not reachable on this path, which is a RESULT. Record it and move to the next candidate rather than escalating payloads blindly.

entries.claim: After a request carrying a __proto__ key, a later request that never repeats the payload shows an inherited property the application never set, which indicates real prototype pollution rather than a rejected input.
steps: Restate the claim as an assertion about observable behaviour.
Identify the ONE request that would be true if the claim holds and false if it does not.
Run it with a control that differs in exactly one variable.
If you cannot name the control, you cannot prove the claim — park it as unverified rather than reporting it.
variation: - **Do two layers disagree about the same bytes?** — container: **do** nest the value one layer deeper (archive, template, include); **observe** a second interpretation after the first check.
- **WHERE does the value arrive?** — cookie: **do** send it in a cookie; **observe** server-side cookie reconstruction.
- **AS whom are you testing?** — low_priv: **do** send as your lowest-privilege account; **observe** whether the response differs from anonymous.
- **What PROVES it, beyond a status code?** — differential: **do** compare against a control that differs in one variable; **observe** the difference the control did not produce.
escalation: No effect raw? Walk the encoding ladder: raw -> percent-encoded -> double-encoded -> look-alike separators, one rung at a time, never all at once.
Flat in the cookie? Move the SAME value to a different location (query / path / body / header / cookie). A filter on one location says nothing about the others.
Flat direct? Go through the real front door (proxy/CDN). Intermediaries normalise, and their normalisation is the behaviour you are hunting.
Still flat? You have proven the sink is not reachable on this path, which is a RESULT. Record it and move to the next candidate rather than escalating payloads blindly.

entries.claim: When an app strips the literal key __proto__ from request bodies, the same pollution succeeds via {"constructor":{"prototype":{"<key>":"<value>"}}} because the prototype is still reachable as obj.constructor.prototype.
steps: Send {"__proto__":{"pp1":"x"}} and check for cross-request inheritance to establish a baseline.
Send {"constructor":{"prototype":{"pp2":"x"}}} to the same endpoint.
On a fresh request, read pp2 and pp1 on a new object.

entries.claim: Prototype pollution is proved by a property that is visible on an object the test never sent any payload to — a freshly constructed `({})` in the same process returning the injected key — because a successful assignment to the prototype is by definition visible through the whole prototype chain.
steps: Record the BASELINE: request the endpoint with a benign, known-good value for the parameter. Save the full response (status, length, body hash).
Change exactly ONE variable: set the parameter to the attack value. Send it again with identical method, headers and cookies.
DIFF the two responses on all three axes: status code, body length, and body content hash.
Attribute every difference. A difference the control did not produce is the finding; a difference the control also produces is the application's normal behaviour.
Then re-run the attack value THREE times to separate a real condition from per-request noise (timing, nonce, ordering).
variation: - **Do two layers disagree about the same bytes?** — single: **do** one parser sees the request; **observe** a consistent rejection or acceptance.
- **What sits between client and sink?** — cached: **do** add a cache-buster, then repeat without; **observe** whether a cached 200 masked the real path.

steps: First establish what the filter rejects: send the plain attack value and record the rejection (status, message, silence).
Then vary ONE encoding dimension at a time: separators, case, trailing dots, alternate separators, redundant segments, container-level normalisation.
The first variation that passes identifies the filter's matching weakness precisely — which is the finding.
Confirm the bypass reaches the sink by observing an EFFECT, not by observing a different response status.
